title: Resolving AdaBoost Cycling with LLMs: A Computer-Assisted Counterexample
claim: A research process unfolded as a sequence of stages, with human decisions and a failed detour leading to the final result.
layout: 2 rows of 3 boxes, left-to-right then wrapping down, arrows between
description: Six rounded-corner boxes in two rows of three, linked by thin black arrows. The top row reads left to right: 'Classical input' (the cycling question, local cycles, balancing identity), 'Solver and critic' (attempts at a convergence proof fail; the fifth summary proposes incompatible rates), and 'Human decision' (pursue the disproof; the solver builds two competing gadgets). An arrow drops from the right end of the top row to the left of the second row. The second row reads left to right: 'A failed route' (a second mode inside one gadget cannot be scheduled independently), 'Exact checks' (state every domain and inequality precisely; check the code against the proof), and 'Later models' (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra simplify the proof and reduce the matrix to 2,500 rows). Each box has a bold title and a short description. It is black and white and text-only, with no icons or color.
caption: How the argument developed, reconstructed from the saved conversation excerpts and later revisions. An early proposal tried to use a second, passive mode within a single gadget, but two modes that are updated together cannot be scheduled independently (while the final construction uses two separate gadgets, which can). The arrows trace the main line of development.
abstract: We develop a computer-assisted counterexample to the open question of whether exhaustive AdaBoost always converges to a finite cycle, posed by Rudin, Schapire, and Daubechies in COLT 2012. The construction is based on a block-product of two small AdaBoost instances whose two factors share an exact period-2 orbit for their five-step branch maps, but whose linearized return maps have dominant eigenvalues with an irrational logarithmic ratio. This irrationality forces the sequence of instances that win each round of updates to have an irrational asymptotic frequency, which precludes convergence to a finite cycle. The resulting counterexample has 2,500 examples, weak-learning margin $1/5$, and a uniform initial distribution, and it holds under every maximizing tie rule. All finite computations in the proof are certified by rational arithmetic in SymPy, with SageMath verifying the main inequalities. We also document the collaborative workflow that led to the construction, in which GPT-5.4 Pro produced the key technical arguments; Claude Opus 4.6 summarized and critiqued different versions of that work, proposing new directions to pursue; and the authors orchestrated the process by selecting directions to prioritize, resolving ambiguities, refining each argument, and verifying the final solution. Later conversations with GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra substantially simplified the solution. We present this as one of the first in-depth case studies of LLM-assisted mathematical research, resolving a long-standing open problem from theoretical machine learning, and detail the advantages and challenges of such research.
